title: Hamsa, the mantra in every breath
hook: a yoga Upanishad hears hamsa in every breath, and teachers turn it into so'ham: I am That
carry: so'ham: every breath says i am that
tomorrow: why would silent japa count most?

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana at sandhya: prayer at the joints of the day: standing until the sun shows, sitting until the stars appear.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA.` · `SANDHYA: PRAYER AT THE JOINTS OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Ha, on the way out. Sa, on the way in. Breathe out slowly through the nose, and the air makes a soft sound, close to an h. Breathe in, and there's a faint hiss, close to an s. Easy to miss; it's just breath. But some yoga texts heard something more. To them, that soft sound was a mantra, repeated day and night by every breathing creature, without anyone choosing to say it.
screen: `HA, ON THE WAY OUT.` → `SA, ON THE WAY IN.` → `A MANTRA NOBODY SAYS.`

segments.voice: The text is the Dhyanabindu Upanishad, one of the yoga Upanishads. In paraphrase: the breath goes out with the sound ha and comes back in with the sound sa, and so the living being is always repeating hamsa, hamsa. This, it says, is called the ajapa gayatri. Ajapa means not-japa: repetition that happens without effort, with no beads, no lips, no count. Hamsa is also the Sanskrit word for a swan or a wild goose, and in Indian poetry the swan can sip the milk out of milk mixed with water. So it became a picture of a soul that can tell the real from the passing, and the greatest renunciates are given the title paramahamsa, the supreme swan. Some teachers turn the sound around: so'ham, I am That. Vedanta teachers hear in those two syllables one of this path's biggest ideas: the Self in you, the atman, is not finally separate from Brahman, the one reality in everything. Read that way, every breathing creature says it all day, a sparrow, a grandmother, a baby asleep, and almost nobody hears. For four days this practice has been about keeping a mantra going: setting terms, counting beads, tying it to dawn and dusk. Ajapa adds something quieter. The repetition isn't only the one you push. It's also the one you finally hear. Some teachers keep the beads and the chosen mantra and let it ride on the breath, one part on the out-breath, one on the in. The discipline stays. It just rides on a sound that was already saying who you are.
screen: `HA OUT, SA IN: HAMSA.` · `AJAPA: THE JAPA NOT DONE.` · `THE SWAN THAT TELLS MILK FROM WATER.` · `SO'HAM: I AM THAT.` · then, large: `THE ATMAN IS NOT SEPARATE FROM BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Let the breath move through the nose, no counting, and listen: a soft ha on the out-breath, a faint sa on the in, not made any louder. If you've been keeping a mantra, let it rest on that sound, part on the out-breath and part on the in; if not, stay with hamsa, or with the breath's own sound. When the mind drifts, come back to listening.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, ajapa: the mantra the breath keeps by itself, hamsa, so'ham, I am That.
Your line: so'ham, every breath says I am That. The atman and Brahman, in two syllables. I'll be here tomorrow.

chat.meaning: The Dhyanabindu Upanishad hears the breath repeat hamsa without effort, the ajapa. Turned around it's so'ham, I am That: many teachers read it as the Self one with Brahman.

tie.story: The Dhyanabindu Upanishad hears every living being breathe out ha and in sa, repeating hamsa without ever choosing to.

tie.you: when today could you stop and hear the breath's own mantra?

hamsa.meaning: a swan or wild goose; also the breath's sound, ha and sa

ajapa.meaning: japa that isn't done: repetition without effort

so'ham.meaning: a turned-around hamsa: I am That

paramahamsa.meaning: the supreme swan, a title for great renunciates
